questions.q: A student's essay recounts her parents' divorce in vivid detail but never arrives at anything. In Gornick's terms, what's missing?
choices: The story: the insight or emotional experience the writer makes of the events
questions.explain: The essay has a situation, what happened, but no story, what it means to the writer.

choices: The context or circumstance: what happened, the plot
questions.explain: The situation is the surface of the piece; the story is what it's really about.

questions.q: Why does Gornick call the narrator of a memoir a 'persona'?
choices: Because the narrator is always a fictional character
Because memoirs should be written in the third person
Because the narrator must be anonymous
Because it's a constructed version of the writer, clear-sighted enough to tell the truth, including about their own part
questions.explain: The everyday self is defensive; the narrator readers can trust is a craft achievement.

questions.q: A narrator who is always wronged and never sees their own part in events usually loses the reader. Why, for Gornick?
choices: The reader can't trust a narrator who can't tell the whole truth
questions.explain: Gornick's truth-speaking narrator must be able to see their own role.

questions.q: Why does much writing about very recent events fail, on Gornick's view?
choices: The writer hasn't yet got the detachment to see the story in the situation
It's written in the present tense
questions.explain: Distance, from time or revision, lets the writer find the story.

questions.q: Which pair best captures the parallel between Gornick and Franklin?
choices: Both say you need to know where a piece arrives: for Franklin a resolution in the world, for Gornick an insight in the writer
Both insist on the inverted pyramid
questions.explain: Each says the piece only works once you know its destination.

questions.q: What did the 2003 debate around Gornick concern?
choices: Whether memoirs may use present tense
Whether combining real incidents or people into composites is acceptable in memoir and reporting
questions.explain: It raised the question of how far a constructed persona and narrative can go before breaking readers' trust.

ideas: Every piece of personal writing has two layers: what happened, and what the writer has come to understand by it.
The 'I' of a memoir is a constructed narrator, wiser and more truthful than the writer's everyday self.
Much weak personal writing recounts events vividly and never discovers what they mean.
